articles.title: Russia resorts to desperate World War One defence technique to protect its oil refineries — floating barrage balloons failed to curtail V1s and are unlikely to succeed against UAVs
articles.summary:
Russia resorts to desperate World War One defence technique to protect its oil refineries — floating barrage balloons failed to curtail V1s and are unlikely to succeed against UAVs
Barrage balloons versus drones
- Russia has updated the concept of barrage balloons to defend oil refineries
- Barrage balloons were first deployed over 100 years ago to defend against air raids
- It is not clear what the measures are defending against, as they only appear suitable for disabling smaller drones
Russia has deployed barrage balloons around its oil refineries to defend against Ukraine drone attacks – but the demonstration using a small drone has raised questions about the effectiveness of the measure.
Protecting oil refineries from drone strikes is key to Russia’s economic strength and supports its efforts in the invasion and occupation of Ukraine. But while the barrage balloons employ intriguing radar-based altitude-adjusting motors to ensure drones are slowed or caught, the deployment seems unsuited to the drones Ukraine would actually send for such a strike.

Les Mousquetaires, which owns the Intermarché chain, said its fridges and freezers were put into defrost and heated to as much as 50°C.
CERT-FR, the French government's computer emergency response team, said in an alert published in French on October 12 that it is aware of numerous compromises affecting two Danfoss controller series, the AK-SM and the AK-SC. It told operators to disconnect the controllers or filter access to them.
CERT-FR is part of ANSSI, France's national cybersecurity agency. ANSSI's head, Vincent Strubel, called it urgent to take the two series off the internet or filter access very tightly, AFP reported.
Neither French authorities nor Danfoss has so far said who carried out the attack or how the attackers got into the controllers. Danfoss said most of the units hit were older models that it no longer updates.

GTA 6 Reportedly Coming to PC in Q1 2027
Rockstar is planning to bring GTA 6 to PC sometime in the first quarter of 2027, according to a new report from GamesBeat. If accurate, PC players would get the game between January and March 2027, just a few months after its November 19 launch on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S. Rockstar still hasn't announced a PC version, and PC was left out of the launch plans from the start. Interestingly, if the timing pans out, that would be a much shorter wait than last time. GTA 5 hit consoles in September 2013 and only reached PC in April 2015, roughly 19 months later. 
This could matter for the roleplay ecosystem too, since FiveM, the framework behind most GTA 5 roleplay servers, runs only on PC, and GTA 6's online mode is already tipped for 2027. Of course, early PC launch windows have surfaced before that haven't exactly panned out. A Corsair executive floated an early 2026 launch last year, a comment Corsair later called speculation, and VGC's Andy Robinson suggested last month that the PC version might show up sooner than people expect. A Q1 2027 release would also arrive before Take-Two's fiscal year closes on March 31, 2027. Until Rockstar says something, readers are advised to treat this as a well-sourced rumor and not a confirmed date.

articles.title: LG Smart TVs Vulnerable to Pre-Auth Root Takeover From Local Network
articles.summary:
Three vulnerabilities in LG's webOS can be chained to give an attacker on the same local network root access to certain smart TVs without a PIN or any interaction from the owner.
LG has issued a fix, according to an advisory published by SSD Secure Disclosure on October 12.
The chain was tested on two TV models, the 32LQ636BPSA and the 27TQ600SW, running webOS 7.5.7-25 on firmware 04.54.40. Whether other models or firmware versions are affected is not known.
Owners of affected TVs should check for a firmware update. No workaround is available for those who cannot update yet.
The attack enters through a service that the TV exposes on port 3001, which is used by the LG ThinQ app for pairing. An attacker replays a manifest from sync-demo, a built-in app already on the device, signed with a test certificate the firmware trusts. A permission in the manifest causes the pairing service to skip the PIN prompt and hand over a privileged key.
With that key, the attacker launches another built-in app, cmp-client, and points it to an attacker-controlled page. The app does not check where it navigates, and the loaded page keeps access to PalmServiceBridge, an internal interface to the TV's system services.
Through that bridge, the attacker calls the system logging service, pmlogd, passing shell commands through an input field the service does not check. Because pmlogd runs as root, the injected command runs as root.

articles.title: [Webinar] How to Stop AI-Driven Privilege Escalation With Runtime Identity Controls
articles.summary:
The dangerous part of a stolen identity isn't always the initial login. It's what an attacker can do with that access next.
With AI accelerating reconnaissance, exploitation of vulnerabilities, and privilege escalation, attackers can move through systems faster than security teams can investigate. A compromised account that looks legitimate at first could become the starting point for a much larger attack.
And that's where traditional identity security faces a serious problem: Checking who gets access isn't enough if you can't control what happens after.
Why Traditional Identity Controls Are Falling Behind
Many identity security controls focus on authentication, permissions, and access policies. But what happens when a trusted identity is compromised, its behavior changes, or an attacker begins exploiting already granted privileges?
That gap becomes more dangerous as AI-powered attacks accelerate.
Attackers can automate parts of the attack chain while defenders are still collecting alerts, investigating activity, and deciding how to respond.
The answer isn't simply detecting attacks faster. It's the ability to evaluate and control access in real time while an identity is actively being used.
This is the idea behind runtime identity security.
In this upcoming expert-led webinar, you'll learn:
- Where attackers find identity gaps across cloud, on-premises, SaaS, and AI environments.

articles.title: Xandr Fined a Record €8.6 Million for Relaying Grindr Data Revealing Sexual Orientation
articles.summary:
The Norwegian Data Protection Authority (DPA) has fined Xandr, an advertising unit owned by Microsoft, €8.6 million ($9.62 million) for illegally relaying Grindr users' sensitive data to advertisers.
The administrative penalty is the largest issued by the data protection watchdog, arguing the case merited a high fine because of the "very serious" nature of the breach. The infringements occurred between July 2018 and April 2020.
"Xandr acted as an intermediary that relayed the personal data of Grindr users in Norway, including data revealing sexual orientation, to potentially thousands of other companies," the Data Protection Authority said in a statement.
The data protection authority said its investigation found that Xandr was a joint controller with Grindr, which meant it was responsible for obtaining users' consent before processing their data.
Instead of ensuring they had the legal basis for their own processing of the data, Xandr pointed fingers at Grindr, stating it assumed the online dating app had collected users' consent to do so," it added.
Xandr was formed by AT&T following its June 2018 acquisition of AppNexus. The name is a reference to Alexander Graham Bell, who founded AT&T in 1885. It was subsequently sold to Microsoft in late December 2021, following which the brand was retired and consolidated under the Microsoft Ads umbrella in June 2023.

articles.title: GitHub Tightens npm Publishing After Flaw Left 1,500+ Packages Vulnerable to Hijacking
articles.summary:
GitHub has taken the step of expiring unvalidated npm trusted publishing configurations 48 hours after creation after researchers found that it was possible for an attacker to push new versions of a different user's package without having to steal their credentials.
"Your configuration becomes validated and exempt from expiry after its first successful publish," the Microsoft-owned subsidiary said. "Changing the repository or project identity requires a new trust relationship with a fresh 48-hour validation window -- ordinary edits don't restart the deadline."
The change contains the risk associated with trusting a repository or project name that changes ownership, GitHub said, adding npm also rejects trusted publishing tokens from GitHub Actions issue_comment events going forward, along with the Existing pull_request_target restriction.
In an update to its documentation, GitHub states that a newly created trusted publisher configuration must complete its first successful publish within two days, which validates the configuration and binds it to the "repository's immutable identity."
The development comes in response to findings from Bloom Security, which discovered a loophole within npm's trusted publishing to take over thousands of packages and trigger a Shai-Hulud-style cascading supply chain attack. The findings were reported to GitHub on June 6, 2026.

An open-source app called DroidDeck is letting Snapdragon-powered Android devices run Valve's Steam client and Windows PC games on the device itself, with no streaming from a PC or the cloud involved. Other solutions like Steam Link stream games from another PC, whereas DroidDeck runs them on the device itself. It loads Valve's ARM64 Linux Steam client in Big Picture mode as a regular Android app, and Windows games go through Valve's ARM64 Proton with x86 translation. Projects like Armada instead replace Android with SteamOS entirely, and DroidDeck needs neither that nor root access. It also handles GPU driver switching, AMD FSR and Snapdragon GSR upscaling, and frame generation through Lossless Scaling.DroidDeck needs Android 9 or newer and fully supports Adreno 730 and newer GPUs, while Adreno 6xx is experimental and Mali, Xclipse, PowerVR, and Adreno 710 are not supported. articles.title: SAP Discloses Critical CVSS 10 Flaw in Cloud SDK for Python Allowing OAuth2 Credential Theft
articles.summary:
A flaw in SAP's Cloud SDK for Python can send an application's OAuth2 client credentials to a server an attacker controls, SAP said in a security advisory on October 13. The flaw affects multi-tenant applications on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) that use the SDK, SAP's official Python client for BTP services. An attacker must be able to control the tenant subdomain, the name such an application passes to the SDK to say which tenant a request is for.
The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-89111 and carries SAP's CVSS score of 10.0 out of 10. The advisory names version 0.45.2, released on August 21, as the fix.
The SDK handles authentication for those services with the application's client credentials, a client ID and a client secret. Version 0.45.2 added a check that rejects any tenant subdomain that is not a simple name.
Six later releases do not apply that check in every case, The Hacker News found. Versions 0.53.0 through 0.55.0, published between September 10 and September 18, skip it when an application calls the SDK's Destination service module.
Version 0.53.0 moved that module onto new shared code for requesting tokens, and that code did not include the check. Version 0.55.1 added it there on September 18.
Passing a tenant subdomain that contains URL delimiters "now raises ValueError immediately instead of silently routing credentials to an attacker-controlled endpoint," the 0.55.1 release notes say.

articles.title: Por qué los auriculares con cable le están ganando la batalla a los inalámbricos
articles.summary:
Los auriculares con cable, esos que parecían condenados a desaparecer tras la llegada del Bluetooth y el fin del conector jack en los teléfonos, están protagonizando un regreso que los números confirman. Según datos de Circana, sus ventas crecieron un 3% en 2025 en Estados Unidos, tras cinco años seguidos de caídas, con una aceleración del 10% en la segunda mitad del año.
En las primeras seis semanas de 2026, los ingresos subieron un 20%, hasta alcanzar niveles similares a los de 2016. Detrás de este repunte hay tanto una cuestión estética, ligada a la generación Z y su gusto por la cultura visual de finales de los noventa, como razones técnicas de peso.
Calidad de sonido: la ventaja técnica de prescindir del Bluetooth
La razón más citada para volver al cable tiene que ver con el sonido. Cuando el audio viaja por Bluetooth, se transmite de forma inalámbrica y suele pasar por un códec que comprime los datos. Ese proceso de compresión introduce una variable que no existe en una conexión por cable, donde la señal llega sin necesidad de ese paso intermedio.
Apple lo explica en sus propios materiales: las conexiones Bluetooth no permiten reproducir audio sin pérdida en condiciones habituales. Para acceder a ese tipo de audio en dispositivos compatibles, es necesario recurrir a una conexión por cable adecuada.

L’adoption massive de l’intelligence artificielle dans les entreprises fait aussi les affaires des cybercriminels. articles.title: El ‘padrino de la IA’ advierte sobre el desarrollo de esta tecnología: “Estamos creando seres extraterrestres”
articles.summary:
Geoffrey Hinton, considerado el “padrino de la inteligencia artificial” por su papel pionero en el desarrollo de las redes neuronales, afirmó en una entrevista con el diario británico The Guardian que la humanidad enfrenta un desafío sin precedentes: “Estamos creando seres de un tipo diferente”, dijo, y agregó que la sociedad dispone de apenas un par de años para adaptarse a esa realidad.
El científico, que trabajó durante años en Google antes de renunciar en 2023 para poder hablar con libertad sobre los riesgos de la tecnología, volvió a insistir en que existe una posibilidad seria de que los sistemas de inteligencia artificial escapen al control humano. Según explicó, no se trata de una predicción cerrada, sino de una advertencia sobre un riesgo que no puede descartarse.
“Si te dicen que hay un 10% de posibilidades de que el autobús choque, no te subís al autobús”, ejemplificó Hinton. “El objetivo de dar números es decir que esto es un riesgo serio. No sabemos cuán serio, pero lo es”.
Un cruce con el CEO de Nvidia
Las declaraciones de Hinton llegan después de un mes marcado por una creciente lista de científicos e investigadores que se sumaron a sus advertencias sobre los peligros de la inteligencia artificial, lo que derivó en la organización apresurada de reuniones en el Congreso de Estados Unidos y en un consenso global poco habitual sobre la necesidad de actuar.

articles.title: Attacker Chains Three Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Days for Root Access, Only Two Patched So Far
articles.summary:
An attacker chained three zero-day flaws in Ivanti Connect Secure, a VPN appliance, to run commands as root without logging in, security firm Volexity said on October 13. Ivanti has released fixes for two of the flaws and told customers on affected versions to "act immediately." A fix for the third is still pending, according to Volexity.
Volexity, which reported the flaws to Ivanti, found the attack on one customer's appliance. The appliance was fully patched at the time and running version 22.8R2.4. The attacker, which Volexity tracks as UTA0576, began exploiting it on October 3.
Ivanti said on October 13 that it is aware of "limited exploitation in the wild."
The first two flaws are an authentication bypass and a remote code execution flaw, tracked together as CVE-2026-104935. Together they let an attacker run code as the appliance's cgi-server user, and the third flaw, a privilege escalation, raises that to root, Volexity said.
The CVE record Ivanti filed shows which Connect Secure versions are affected:
- Affected: Connect Secure "before version 25.1.3.0"
- Not affected: version 22.7R2.14 "or prior"
- Listed as unaffected: versions 22.8R2.5, 25.1.3.0 and 25.1.3.1
Ivanti's security advisory has more on the affected versions and the fixes.
The release notes for 25.1.3.0 are dated July 2026. Customers already on that version are outside the range the CVE record gives.

articles.title: AI isn't enough: Why store infrastructure will determine which retailers scale successfully
articles.summary:
AI isn't enough: Why store infrastructure will determine which retailers scale successfully
Why AI success in retail depends on infrastructure
The hardest part of retail AI may soon be the part nobody puts in the demo.
A model can recommend a markdown, predict a stockout, adjust a picking route or identify a pattern in store traffic in milliseconds. But a retailer only gets value when that decision becomes an accurate action in the physical store. Whether it’s a price change or a sensor reading, it has to arrive promptly for it to be useful.
SVP for SOLUM, Europe.
There is already a striking gap between AI ambition and execution. Deloitte's 2026 survey of 200 retail and consumer products executives found that 75% consider AI a top strategic priority, yet only 16.5% can quantify the return they are getting from it. Clearly, retailers believe in AI. The harder problem is turning isolated capabilities into something that works consistently across the business.
For physical retailers, the challenge does not end with models, data or software. AI-driven decisions have to pass through stores containing thousands of devices, existing networks and years of installed technology. In complex environments, the building itself can affect connectivity. As the number of connected endpoints grows, so does the importance of the wireless foundation carrying information across the store.

articles.title: Docker Fixes Critical Two-Year-Old Hub Flaw That Let One User Push Images as Another
articles.summary:
A flaw in Docker Hub, the registry where container images are published and downloaded, let one user push, pull, or delete images as another user. Docker fixed the flaw on September 30 and says it found no evidence that anyone exploited it.
The flaw was in the feature that converts a personal account into an organization, Docker said in a security advisory on October 12. Conversion transferred the account's personal access tokens (PATs) to the user designated as the organization's owner. A PAT is used in place of a password in the registry, and the person who created each token can still use it.
The access was limited to the registry. It did not reach the Docker Hub web interface, and it could not be used to change a password, email address, or two-factor settings, or to take over an account.
Docker tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-105445 and rated it critical. The CVE record it published on October 13 gives the flaw a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.4.
The flaw was open from August 26, 2024, until the fix, a little over two years. Docker made the fix on Docker Hub itself, so there is no update to install.
Docker Hub cannot move a repository from one account to another. A user instead converts a personal account into an organization that keeps the same name, and must name an existing account as its owner.

El paciente, operado en mayo en Sídney, ya leyó una palabra con el dispositivo.

La cirugía, de aproximadamente una hora, se realizó en el Hospital de Ojos de Sídney bajo la supervisión del médico Matthew Simunovic. Forma parte de PRIMAlia, un ensayo registrado bajo el identificador NCT07266584 que comenzó a reclutar pacientes el 22 de abril y prevé incorporar a cinco personas con Stargardt, retinosis pigmentaria u otras degeneraciones retinianas hereditarias.
Para participar, los pacientes deben tener un diagnóstico confirmado de degeneración retiniana hereditaria que afecte la mácula de ambos ojos, según los criterios de inclusión registrados para el estudio. El ensayo tiene fecha de finalización primaria en marzo de 2029 y de cierre total en 2031.

articles.title: Anthropic Warns Small AI Models Could Soon Form Self-Propagating IoT Botnets
articles.summary:
Small artificial intelligence (AI) models may be months away from developing capabilities to self-replicate on IoT devices like smart ovens and off-brand Android TV boxes, according to a warning from Anthropic.
The frontier AI lab said small AI models could form autonomous, self-propagating worm botnets that are "challenging to shut down," since "there's no centralized point to shut off."
Prior work has demonstrated that AI agents can act like one by scanning their network, executing an exploit, and copying model weights to a target machine across a GPU cluster with an aim to generate tailored attack strategies and use compromised machines as a botnet to run large language models (LLMs) in order to sustain its reasoning and expand in scale.
"Such an 'AI worm' could carry its model weights with it as it reproduces (or re-download them from a public hub), and then run inference directly on compromised hardware," Anthropic said. "Effectively, the weights would become part of the malware payload."
The idea, at a high level, explains how AI models could potentially break into internet-connected devices and use their computing power to run themselves and spread to other devices, without having to rely on expensive data centers all the time. A more powerful model that's too large to fit into a single device could be split into small chunks and run across multiple machines to collectively run it.

AI Agents are unlike any software development witnessed before. Traditionally, trustworthy software systems have followed a structured approach to being built and developed. One that plans, builds, tests, and maintains software to ensure its reliability and scalability. This created the Software Development LifeCycle (SDLC) (1) framework.
But AI agents are different: they are a team of autonomous, probabilistic actors that work most effectively in a real-time, event-driven environment, enabling the agents to coordinate with real-time data to develop, learn, and work.
Director of AI and industry solutions at Solace.
To scale an enterprise workforce of AI agents, organizations need to combine the principles of employee management with software development rigor. These agents are not static software that can be coded and developed, due to probabilistic language models. They are built, evaluated, and governed differently.

articles.title: Four-Byte Write and Timing Bug Let Researchers Run Code in Windows SmartScreen Enclave
articles.summary:
Security researchers ran their own code inside a protected part of Windows that is meant to stay sealed off even when the rest of the computer is taken over.
The protected area is a VBS enclave, an isolated slice of memory the operating system uses to guard secrets, and the one they broke into handles passwords for a Windows anti-phishing feature.
The work was done in a lab as a proof of concept, has not been seen in real attacks, and Microsoft fixed the flaw in its September 8, 2026 update.
The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-83498. Microsoft rates it an elevation-of-privilege issue, Critical, with a CVSS score of 7.8, and says it has not been exploited and was not publicly known before the fix. Microsoft also says it found the same issue internally. The research, by the security firm Doyensec, was published October 13, more than a month after the patch.
A VBS enclave is a signed library that a normal Windows program loads but cannot read or change once it is running. The Windows hypervisor keeps the enclave's memory in a more trusted world, called VTL1 or Isolated User Mode, that ordinary code in the normal world, VTL0, cannot reach, according to Microsoft.
The design is meant to protect what is inside even if an attacker has already taken over the normal kernel or is running as SYSTEM. Running attacker-chosen code inside that world is what makes this research notable.

articles.title: AI-Found Linux Kernel Flaw Gives Local Users Root, and Can Break a Guest Out to the Host
articles.summary:
A flaw in Linux's vhost subsystem lets a local user read and write kernel memory at will and become root across nearly a decade of kernel versions. In one virtualization setup, it lets an untrusted virtual machine write to the host's memory and hijack the program that runs the virtual machine.
The bug is tracked as CVE-2026-74580 and named Vghost. Tencent Zhuque Lab, which found the flaw, released a fix on August 3 and published a full write-up on October 12 with working demos of both attacks. There is no public sign it has been exploited yet.
vhost is the part of the Linux kernel that speeds up network and other input/output for virtual machines and containers. A local user reaches it by opening a device node, usually /dev/vhost-net or /dev/vhost-vsock.
On the host, the flaw gives an unprivileged user a reliable way to read and write any kernel address, bypass KASLR, and escalate to root. The attack is deterministic: it needs no memory grooming and no lucky timing.
The second attack is narrower. When a virtual machine's virtio device is placed behind a virtual IOMMU with iommu_platform turned on, and vhost runs in device-IOTLB mode, an untrusted guest can trigger the same bug and make the host kernel write out of bounds into the host's QEMU process. From there, a guest can overwrite a function pointer in QEMU and take control of where the host process runs next, or crash it.

The bug was simple: the login let you choose where your sign-in code went. Proving it on a live website was the hard part.
TL;DR
- During an authorized assessment, an AI pentesting agent found a critical authentication bypass on a major insurer's production website, on its own.
- One login request let the user choose where the one-time passcode went.
- The attack was the easy part. Proving it on a live site took web context built over a decade.
The Login Worked. Then the Agent Stopped.
Reflectiz's AI pentesting agent was mapping the login flow of a major insurer's production website, which has millions of users.
The agent requested a login code and directed it to an email inbox it controlled. The code arrived. The login went through. Its guardrails halted the test after the login succeeded.
The agent had discovered a critical-severity authentication bypass on its own. Reflectiz reported it to the insurer.
The Flaw: The Request Chose Where the Code Went
A one-time passcode (OTP) only proves who you are if it goes somewhere already linked to the account. Here, that link was broken.
The login request carried two fields that decided delivery: the channel and the address. Normally, the code went by text to the phone number on the account. But the request could change the channel. Switch it to email, and the server sent the code to whatever address the request named, not the address registered to the account.

Data center boom across Europe could well lead to higher electricity prices, report warns
Europe could be next to face data center-related price hikes
- Report warns Europe's data center push ultimately means the sector will need more electricity
- Data centers only pay for their direct upgrades – not broader grid upgrades
- Government intervention is likely needed to protect billpayers
New Moody's data has warned that Europe's growing data center footprint could severely impact energy prices across the continent as we're already seeing in the US.
As of 2025, Europe's data center-related electricity consumption stood at around 2.5% of the entire continent's consumption, however within the space of a decade (by 2035), this could more than double to 5.7% across countries like France and the UK.
But more worryingly, the countries that are set to play host to the most capacity will likely see even starker rises, including the Northlands (17%) and Ireland (30%).
European data centers could push energy prices up
Moody's explained that, while data centers would typically pay for any upgrades needed for their direct connection, the grid operator usually picks up the bill for wider network reinforcement. Those additional costs, as well as a tighter supply-demand imbalances, could push costs onto the end user – you and I.

articles.title: Valve deja de fabricar las gafas Index: qué pasará con quienes ya las tienen
articles.summary:
Valve ha dejado de fabricar las gafas de realidad virtual Valve Index, un visor que llegó al mercado el 28 de junio de 2019 y que durante más de siete años fue la principal apuesta de la compañía para jugar en realidad virtual desde Steam. La decisión coincide con la llegada de Steam Frame, el nuevo dispositivo de Valve, y abre dudas entre quienes ya tienen el equipo, los controles y las estaciones base.
La empresa ha comunicado que los propietarios de las Index mantendrán la compatibilidad con Steam y SteamVR, además del acceso al soporte técnico. Por tanto, el fin de la fabricación no implica que el visor deje de funcionar ni que los juegos adquiridos queden inutilizados. El cambio afecta a la producción y a la disponibilidad de nuevo hardware.
Las unidades restantes se venderán hasta que se agote el inventario
Valve confirmó que ya no produce nuevos visores, mandos ni accesorios de Valve Index. Los equipos que todavía permanecen en stock seguirán a la venta con descuento, aunque solo hasta que se terminen las existencias disponibles.
La compañía no ha anunciado una fecha para retirar esos productos de su tienda. El proceso dependerá de la cantidad de unidades que queden en cada mercado. En España, la página del dispositivo no muestra actualmente una opción de compra, lo que apunta a que la disponibilidad ya es limitada o inexistente en ese territorio.

articles.title: Researchers Used a Public OpenAI Model to Build a $250,000 Chrome Full-Chain Exploit in Six Days
articles.summary:
A team at security firm XBOW chained three then-unknown Google Chrome bugs into a single attack that runs code on a Windows computer when the user only loads a web page, the company said.
Its researchers built the attack in six days by directing AI agents running OpenAI's publicly available GPT-5.6 Sol model. Google has since confirmed all three bugs, fixed them, and paid XBOW its top $250,000 reward for a full Chrome exploit.
The attack is a full chain: a set of bugs used together to break every layer of Chrome's protection, from a web page all the way to the computer.
Chrome runs web page code inside two nested sandboxes, the barriers that stop a hacked page from reaching the rest of the machine. The chain crossed both. The result was code running outside Chrome on Windows, with no need for the user to click or download anything.
All three bugs are now fixed, and XBOW says they were never used against Chrome users. The two that carry public identifiers were fixed in Chrome 152.0.7977.65 on August 25 and 152.0.7977.82 on September 3.
Chrome updates on its own, but the fix only takes effect after the browser restarts, so the action is to relaunch Chrome and confirm the version is 152.0.7977.82 or later.
The six days are the headline, and they need their frame. XBOW built the awarded chain between Sunday, August 2, and Friday, August 7, during the Black Hat and DEF CON conferences in Las Vegas. That sprint followed months of earlier work: the company set the challenge at a Jan…

articles.title: How to Run a Deepfake Readiness Drill Before a Cloned Voice Calls Your Team
articles.summary:
Cloned voices and synthetic video calls now show up in payment fraud, help desk resets, and access requests. A structured drill shows security teams exactly where verification breaks down, while nothing is at stake.
The call comes in at 4:40 on a Friday. It's the CFO, or it sounds exactly like her, asking the controller to push a supplier payment out before the weekend because a deal closes Monday. She's traveling, she's rushed, and she apologizes for the bad connection. Ten minutes later an email lands with the wire details.
A couple of years ago that scenario was a conference talk. Now it shows up in incident reports. In a 2025 Gartner survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders, 62% said their organization had experienced at least one deepfake attack in the prior 12 months. In the same survey, 43% reported at least one deepfake audio call incident and 37% had run into deepfakes on video calls.
And the wire is only the obvious ask. The same cloned voice can call the help desk to move an MFA token, or ask an identity admin to set up a new global admin ahead of an "audit." A fraudulent wire tends to surface at reconciliation. A quietly added admin account can sit there for months.
Most organizations have a policy that says to verify unusual payment and access requests. Far fewer have checked whether that policy survives a phone call from someone who sounds like the person who signs off on everyone's paycheck. A deepfake readiness drill is how you find out, on your own schedule, with …

articles.title: curl Patches HTTP/2 Upload Flaw After PoC Demonstrates Client-Side Code Execution
articles.summary:
A flaw in how curl handles HTTP/2 uploads lets a malicious server receiving an upload corrupt the client's memory, and the researcher who reported it turned that into code execution on the uploading machine.
The curl project fixed it on October 14 in curl 8.23.0. Taking over a client needs exact knowledge of its build and memory layout, and curl expects a real attack to end in a crash instead.
The flaw, a use-after-free tracked as CVE-2026-92392, affects curl and libcurl 8.12.0 through 8.22.0, both the command-line tool and the library that many other programs use for transfers. curl rates it High on its own four-level scale, its first High-severity flaw since the SOCKS5 heap overflow of October 2023. The project cut its release cycle by two weeks to ship the fix.
The attack runs from the server side. The client has to upload a file of roughly 135KB over HTTP/2 to a server controlled by the attacker, and the server's certificate must pass the client's checks. libcurl negotiates HTTP/2 by default for https:// URLs when the server offers it, and the library was built with HTTP/2 support.
The flaw has shipped in every curl release since 8.12.0 in February 2025. No source reports attacks that use it. The reporter's HackerOne write-up, with the malicious server script and a Docker container described as reproducing the code execution, became public on October 14 with the advisory.

articles.title: Un informe revela que solo 2 de 134 modelos de IA superaron las pruebas sobre terrorismo y armas nucleares
articles.summary:
Un informe del grupo británico Tech Against Terrorism, creado y respaldado por las Naciones Unidas, probó 134 modelos de inteligencia artificial con más de 200 pedidos vinculados a ataques terroristas y armas químicas o nucleares. Solo dos superaron la prueba sin fallas, según el reporte compartido en exclusiva con la revista Wired.
Los investigadores repitieron cada pedido de tres formas distintas. Primero se presentaron como terroristas que buscaban esa información de manera explícita. Después plantearon el mismo pedido como una actividad clandestina. Por último dijeron ser investigadores de seguridad.
Esa diferencia de encuadre cambió todo. Cuando los autores se identificaron como terroristas, los modelos respondieron con información útil en menos del 2% de los casos. Cuando se presentaron como investigadores, ese porcentaje trepó a 16,9%, casi nueve veces más, sin que mediara ninguna prueba de esa supuesta identidad.
Adam Hadley, director ejecutivo de Tech Against Terrorism, presentó los resultados la semana pasada. “Lo que nos resulta un poco absurdo es que hay tanto debate sobre el riesgo existencial, pero muy poca discusión pública sobre los modelos despojados de sus filtros”, dijo. “Mientras el Congreso piensa en una superinteligencia, nadie piensa en la emergencia de la abliteración”.

articles.title: Lack of promised profit could tank the global economy if the AI bubble pops, IMF warns
articles.summary:
Lack of promised profit could tank the global economy if the AI bubble pops, IMF warns
IMF warns of widespread disruption
- IMF warns that an AI market correction could have major economic implications
- Circular investments are making tech companies more intertwined
- A major cyberattack could impact multiple organizations at once
The International Monetary Fund has warned global financial markets are becoming increasingly vulnerable to the volatility of AI investments.
While AI-related investments have becoming an increasingly important driver of economy activity, even helping to offset some of the economic damage associated with ongoing geopolitical upheaval, AI holds the potential of causing major market disruption.
Specifically, the IMF warned of three potential developments – a correction in AI-related investments and company valuations, an increase in government bond yields, or a major cyberattack targeting critical national infrastructure, including financial institutions.
Could an AI market correction lead to widespread disruption?

A GPT Image 2 upscale prompt should start with what must survive the edit. A small image can become larger and more polished while changing a person’s features, a product label or a background detail. Decide whether you need extra pixels for display or are comfortable with a new interpretation of the picture.
Those goals call for different tools. Conventional resizing, a dedicated photo enhancer and a generative image edit may all produce larger files. The important question is what happens to the content along the way.
Check whether the original really needs an AI edit
Find the largest original before doing anything else. A thumbnail copied from a webpage is a poor starting point when the full photograph is still on your phone. Keep that original untouched and make a working copy. Record its width and height in pixels so you can check what the finished file actually delivers.
If you simply need a larger version with the same composition, start with a resizing tool. Adobe describes resampling as changing pixel dimensions by adding or removing pixels. During enlargement, the software estimates the new pixels; increasing their number does not recover information that the camera never recorded.
